observation: Bulk data replication across multiple cloud regions and providers is essential for data analytics, disaster recovery, and geo-distributed model serving, yet cloud multicast can be expensive due to per-GB network egress fees and slow due to cloud network constraints. Egress prices vary by up to 23× across region pairs, with intra-cloud egress costing $0.01–$0.19 per GB and inter-cloud egress costing $0.08–$0.23 per GB, and cross-region bandwidth varies by up to 202×. Cloud providers impose per-VM egress/ingress limits (for example, AWS throttles egress to 5 Gbps per VM), so a single source VM is often the bottleneck, while users must still meet target replication times. Existing throughput-oriented multicast optimizers do not handle monetary cost, and existing cost-aware multicast work either ignores throughput or assumes a capacity-based pricing model that is inconsistent with today's per-GB egress pricing.

claims: Centralized software-defined WAN controllers have shown that inter-datacenter transfer capacity can be scheduled dynamically to improve utilization and meet bandwidth demands.

These systems formulate traffic engineering in terms of bandwidth allocation and aggregate flow demands; they do not incorporate the per-GB egress charges that a cloud customer pays when data leaves a region or provider.

claims: Overlay multicast systems organize end hosts into trees or meshes to provide multi-point distribution without relying on IP multicast.
High-bandwidth dissemination systems optimize the use of available upload and download bandwidth among participants to maximize throughput.
These systems do not model monetary transfer charges or per-VM egress caps imposed by cloud providers, treating bandwidth as the only scarce resource.

claims: Classical multicast routing research formulates distribution-tree construction as a Steiner-tree problem where each link has a fixed cost or weight.
The fixed per-link cost abstraction does not represent usage-sensitive, per-GB egress pricing that commercial clouds charge for traffic leaving a region or provider.
Cloud-of-clouds storage systems replicate or erasure-code data across multiple providers to achieve durability and availability while accounting for provider pricing.
These systems target long-lived object and file replicas at storage services, so they do not address deadline-constrained replay or bulk fan-out from a single source VM to many receiving regions.
